newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-ERA eyes Jabiluka uranium mine study.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-ERA eyes Jabiluka uranium mine study.

text.p: Uranium miner Energy Resources of Australia Ltd (ERA) said on Friday it would release a draft environmental impact statement for its planned Jabiluka uranium mine in the Northern Territory on October 17.
The statement examines a number of options and identifies two main options for development of the Jabiluka Number Two deposit, containing 90,400 tonnes of uranium oxide, ERA said.
Environmentalists have criticised ERA's plans to mine the orebody, which borders the Kakadu National Park.
However, ERA said the mine would take up only a fraction of the park and out of site from a nearby tourist road.
"ERA's preferred option is to mill the Jabiluka ore at Ranger, which would ensure there was minimal environmental impact," ERA chief executive Phillip Shirvington said.
"Under this proposal, the mine site will disturb less than 20 hectares of land," he said in a statement.
Under the option, ore would be trucked on a road contained in the mine site, Shirvington said.
Tailings would be placed in open pits, which would be rehabilitated at the end of the mine life he said.
ERA has said it would be looking to increase its sales of uranium to France, the world's biggest uranium buyer after Paris last month endorsed a ban on tests of nuclear weapons.

Rival miner RTZ-CRA is seeking to develop the Western Australia Kintyre uranium deposit, located on the edge of the remote Great Sandy Desert, adjacent to the Ruddall River National Park, Australia's largest park.
Also WMC Ltd plans to lift uranium production from its Olympic Dam in South Australia to about 3,700 tonnes a year from 1,500 currently.
ERA is 68.4 percent owned by Australian mining and forestry group North Ltd.
Lifting of a 13-year ban on new uranium mines earlier this year is providing Australian companies with an opportunity to participate in a resurgence in demand for the metal.
Analysts estimate uranium currently fetches about US$16.00 a pound, up from $12.00 a year ago, and could go higher as more nuclear power plants are built around the world.
South Korea alone plans to build 19 nuclear power plants as part of a long-term effort to keep pace with growing demand for power, Korea Electric Power Corp has said.

However, in the United States, a proposal by Connecticut Yankee Atomic Power Co to shut down a reactor is being cited by some industry analysts as the most recent example of a troubled industry, at least in a deregulated U.S. power market.
"Connecticut Yankee was built under the protection of regulation and supported by regulation," Raymond Moore, securities analyst at Dillon Read in New York, said earlier.
"Now nuclear plants are no longer economical at selling power into a competitive market," he said.
"The success of these plants depended on their economy of scale. What we've had is just the opposite. Small (generating) units can be built at overall rates much cheaper," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
